studies.title: The Prayer That Opens Everything
studies.meaning: These seven lines are a prayer God teaches so that a person knows how to address Him. Praise comes first, then two names of mercy, then ownership of the day accounts are settled. Only halfway through does the speech turn from talking about God to talking to Him, and only then does it ask. The one request is for direction rather than for relief or wealth, and the commentators read the rest of the Quran as its answer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and among the earliest complete surahs given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), from the years when a small and pressured community was learning to pray at all. A minority of classical reports place a second revelation of it in Medina, and the commentators note the difference without resolving it. From the first written collections it stood at the head of the codex rather than in order of revelation.

keyTerms.note: The definite article makes it total. Not an act of praise that someone chooses to offer, but praise as such, all of it, belonging to God whether or not anyone gives it.
Built on a root shared with the word for womb. It names a mercy that is vast, prior, and unearned, spread over everything created, and the Quran uses it almost as a second name.
Not a narrow footpath but a wide public road, the kind a caravan travels. The word carries openness and ease of passage, so the request is for a road wide enough to walk without stumbling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived by the road. Merchants left for Syria in summer and Yemen in winter, and a caravan's survival turned on whether the guide knew the route across country where a wrong turn meant days without water. Asking to be shown a straight road was not first a metaphor. It was the most practical request a traveller could make, and this prayer puts it in the mouth of everyone who says it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only surah spoken entirely from the human side to God rather than from God to humanity, which is why the commentators describe it as a prayer taught rather than a message sent. The classical tradition records more than twenty names for it, including the Mother of the Book, the Cure, and the Seven Oft-Repeated named in surah fifteen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting praise, mercy and judgement ahead of the request sets an order the whole Quran keeps: God is known before He is asked. The plural voice leaves no room for a purely private religion, since even someone praying alone speaks as part of a community. And the request itself concedes that guidance is not something a person manufactures and keeps. It is asked for daily by people who already have it.

crossReferences.why: Names this surah the seven oft-repeated verses, given alongside the whole of the Quran.
Calls the straight path God's own and warns against the side roads that scatter travellers.
Ties worship to remembrance, the movement this prayer makes from acknowledging God to standing before Him.

studies.applyIt: You probably say these lines several times a day, faster than you can think them. Tomorrow, slow down at the sixth line, the request for a straight road, and hold it for one extra breath before moving on. Notice what you were about to ask for instead. The order of this prayer was given before the asking, and it is worth arriving at the request unhurried.
